description: Although a national flag was foreign to local tradition, it seems banners with the colours yellow, red and green were flown. The colours red, yellow and green had special importance since at least the early 17th Century. It was a symbol of the Ethiopian Empire’s Solomonic dynasty with a connection to the Holy Trinity.

It seems that a banner, depicting the Imperial symbol, the Lion of Judah bearing a cross, has been reported in 1853 in what was usually called Abyssinia in the outside world. It could not be considered a national flag, as the concept was alien to the local population.

The first flag known of the Empire of Ethiopia was probably introduced under European influence, from 1875 when Yohannes IV unified the country by uniting his kingdom, Tigray, with that of Menelik II, King of Shewa (Showa, central Ethiopia). It could be called an imperial banner. The colours purple (amethyst) and white were of Tigrinya origin and disappeared after 1881. The central emblem, with a somewhat rudimentary design, represents the Lion of Judah (the emperor was considered a descendant of that biblical tribe, the same as Jesus), holding a rod with the Christian cross, decorated with ribbons, in his right hand.

In 1881 three coloured pennants, with red on top, was in use in Ethiopia. Not really a “national flag”, it was a symbol of the sovereign, Emperor Yohannes IV. After his death in 1889, when Menelik II succeeded him, the banner was used less frequently, because it was considered a distinctive sign of the deceased sovereign. It was no longer seen by 1904.

On 6 October 1897, after having defeated the Italian army at the Battle of Adowa (Adwa) the year before, Emperor Menelik II decided to adopt a national flag, combining the three pennants into rectangles.  On the central stripe is the first letter of Menelik’s name in Amharic script.

Emperor Menelik II died on 12 December 1913 and the following year the sequence of the flag’s colours, that had sometimes varied, were firmly fixed with green at the top. The colours were interpreted as having a connection to the Holy Trinity and the three main provinces. They could stand for: green - the country’s fertile land and hope, yellow - natural wealth and the Christian church, red - power and faith of the nation.

On 3 October 1935, the Italian Fascist regime under Mussolini attacked Ethiopia and occupied it for five years. Emperor Haile Selassie had to flee abroad into exile in 1936, and on 9 May that year Italy annexed the country, and the Italian flag was hoisted. It was modelled on that of revolutionary France at the end of the 18th Century, with green substituted for blue. The tricolour was officially adopted for the Kingdom of Sardinia with the arms of Savoy in its centre. It was the basis of the flag of a united Italy.

During the Fascist Italian occupation of Ethiopia until 1941, Emperor Haile Selassie lived in exile in the United Kingdom and the Italian king, Vittorio Emmanuele III, had proclaimed himself Emperor of Ethiopia. The Italian State flag featured the crown of the House of Savoy, which ruled Italy from 1861 to 1946.

In 1941 Italy was defeated, and Haile Selassie restored to the throne. The Ethiopian flag was restored as the national flag on 5 May 1941. A Royal State flag was introduced on that day as well, featuring the crowned Lion of Judah, carrying a cross in the central stripe. The three coloured pennants fly from the cross. The flag is a link between the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, the peoples, and the nation.

In 1949 a Royal Standard was introduced that also could function as a War Flag. On the obverse side it depicts the Lion of Judah, encircled by the collar of the Order of Solomon’s Seal; in each corner of the Standard is the badge of the order, a Star of Solomon or David with a cross. The inscription in Amharic script reads “The victorious Lion of the tribe of Judah”.

The Royal Standard of 1949 that also could function as a War Flag depicts on the reverse side St. George slaying the dragon, encircled by the collar of the Order of Solomon’s Seal. In each corner is the badge of the order, a Star of Solomon or David with a cross. The inscription in Amharic script reads “Great Star of Honour”, although this was not always displayed.

On 12 September 1974, the Derg military junta deposed Emperor Haile Selassie and declared that Crown Prince Asfaw Wossen would be anointed “King” upon his return from abroad. This never happened and in January 1975 Ethiopia’s State flag of green-yellow-red with the imperial lion was modified by removing the crown from the lion’s head and changing the Cross finial to a spear point, symbolising that the powers of the monarchy and the church were eliminated. The lion was also no longer “Lion of Judah” but “Lion of Ethiopia”.

In January 1975 the War Flag, (previously also the Royal Standard) was changed: the obverse side was the same as the State flag, with the uncrowned lion, and on the reverse side only the figure of St. George slaying the dragon. In March 1975 the monarchy was abolished, a republic proclaimed, and both flags disappeared.

The National flag of Ethiopia was, from 1914, always a plain green-yellow-red tricolour. In 1975 the Derg military junta also proclaimed it the official flag. The symbolism of the colours may vary but could mean: green - symbolising hope, or the land and its fertility; yellow - peace and harmony between Ethiopia’s various ethnic and religious groups; red - blood spilled in defence of Ethiopia.

On 12 September 1975, the Socialist military “Derg” regime adopted a flag featuring a new State Arms, designed by Tadesse Mesfin. It depicted a traditional plough, emphasising the importance of agriculture, a cogwheel suggesting industry and the 14 administrative districts; attached to the plough is a sling, shaped like the first letter of the Amharic alphabet, emphasising education. A spear, sword and shield, superimposed by a lion symbolise defence. Branches of yellowwood and wild olive frame the emblem. At the top is “Provisional Military Government of Socialist Ethiopia” in Amharic script.

In 1987, through a referendum, Ethiopia became a People’s Democratic Republic. Mengistu Haile Mariam was confirmed as president. On 12 September 1987, the State Flag flag now carried a circular blue shield. It featured a stele of the ancient Kingdom of Aksum, a cogwheel, a red ribbon depicting a golden lion’s head, a spear and a sceptre. In a red circle was a yellow star, emanating 39 yellow rays. The country’s name was at the top in Amharic script.

In May 1991 the oppressive Communist regime of Mengistu Haile Mariam came to an end when forces from the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front entered Addis Ababa, and Mengistu fled. A plain flag was used from then on by the Transitional Government. Flags without emblems had always been used by the populace, irrespective of which government was in power.

On 28 May 1992, the Transitional Government of Ethiopia adopted a State Flag with its emblem, in green, white and black on the central stripe. It features a pigeon, scales, an ornamental gate, surrounded by a wreath and a cogwheel, symbolising industry.

In May 1995, after multiparty elections, the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia came into being and on 6 February 1996, its flag was adopted. It features on the central stripe a light blue disk, symbolising peace, and a pentagram with rays emanating from its inner angles signifying “the bright prospect in sight for the Nations, Nationalities and Peoples (of Ethiopia) united in their common will”.

On 31 October 1996 the central emblem was modified: On the central stripe of the green-yellow-red flag it now features a larger and darker blue disk, symbolising peace, and a pentagram with rays emanating from its inner angles signifying “the bright prospect in sight for the Nations, Nationalities and Peoples (of Ethiopia) united in their common will”. In 2009 the present flag was made mandatory and was no longer to be displayed without its emblem, although plain flags may still be seen.
